Findings converge on ReconnectPolicy's first-occurrence, type-keyed Slow classification
findings.why_it_matters: `ReconnectPolicy.on_failure` picks Fast or Slow from a single exception's type, on its first occurrence, with no history. The one exception is the 1009 streak (`websocket_reconnect.py:192`), the only place where recurrence counts. Findings 4 and 5 are transient restart signatures (a Traefik 404, a TLS EOF mid-handshake) that hit the 5-minute Slow tier on first sight. Finding 6 is a deterministic failure (an unexpected exception that recurs identically) that never leaves Fast. Each finding proposes its own local edit: drop 404, narrow the SSL match, add a streak counter for unexpected exceptions. The question for you is whether this classification mechanism (type lists deciding the tier on first occurrence) should be re-evaluated, which includes whether recurrence rather than type should decide entry to Slow, or patched list by list. D9 already came out of a convergence re-evaluation in the sketch challenge (design.md:151), so re-evaluating reopens a decision that has been ratified twice.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the type-keyed classification and address Findings 4, 5 and 6 individually.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the type-keyed classification and address Findings 4, 5 and 6 individually.

findings.title: Findings converge on WebsocketService reusing lifecycle readiness as its connection-status display
findings.why_it_matters: HA connection status reaches users through the lifecycle readiness pair, `ready_event` plus `_ready_reason`. It is written by `report_not_ready`, which sets the private `_ready_reason` directly to get around `mark_not_ready`'s first-reason-wins rule (`websocket_service.py:401-412`). It is also gated by a "never-connected stays lifecycle-ready" exception (`:384-387`), which the RUNNING gate itself breaks (`:468`). The three findings:
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate how `WebsocketService` reports HA connection status before addressing Findings 9, 10 and 11 individually. Open questions: should connection status ride on lifecycle readiness at all? What does lifecycle readiness mean for a service that has never connected? Which channel does the live UI read for connection status? Does `report_not_ready`, with its private-field write, need to exist? How much of this belongs to #1926?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate how WebsocketService reports HA connection status before addressing Findings 9, 10 and 11 individually.
findings.choice_reason: R1 now (lifecycle-only readiness, reason carries status); R2 typed wire state belongs in #1926 (commented)

findings.title: A never-connected `auth_invalid` parks permanently, which strands the ledger's own cold-boot clock-skew case and removes main's restart-policy self-heal
findings.why_it_matters: D3 uses the in-memory `has_ever_connected` to infer that a token never worked. The ledger's clock-skew assumption (an HA host booting with its clock behind the token's `iat`) describes a host reboot. That reboot usually restarts Hassette too, so `has_ever_connected` is False and a valid token parks at once and stays parked (`websocket_reconnect.py:184`). AUTH_FAILED has no way out short of a process restart (design.md:208), and health reports `starting`, the same as a slow boot (see Finding 7).
findings.recommended: A: Give a never-connected token the same 3 retries 60 s apart before parking, by dropping the `not has_ever_connected` condition at `websocket_reconnect.py:184`.
findings.chosen: A: Give a never-connected token the same 3 retries 60 s apart before parking, by dropping the `not has_ever_connected` condition at `websocket_reconnect.py:184`.

findings.title: A handshake 404 goes straight to the 5-minute Slow tier, and 404 is the normal restart signal behind Traefik
findings.why_it_matters: D2 and D8 exist so that Hassette recovers within seconds of HA returning. D9 sends a handshake 404 to Slow on its first occurrence, even when the connection that just dropped had been stable for days. Behind Traefik, the usual Docker Compose front end, the router disappears with a stopped backend container and Traefik answers 404 until the container is back. That behavior comes from both critics' knowledge of Traefik and was not verified in this repo. So a 40 s HA restart can cost up to 5 minutes of downtime, with an ERROR row on every attempt. The ledger accepted "up to 5 min to notice an upstream fix for 4xx", but in this topology the 404 is the restart itself, not an upstream fault.
findings.recommended: A: Remove 404 from `SLOW_HANDSHAKE_STATUSES` so it retries on the Fast curve.
findings.chosen: A: Remove 404 from `SLOW_HANDSHAKE_STATUSES` so it retries on the Fast curve.

findings.title: Every `ssl.SSLError` is Slow, including transient handshake EOF and reset, not only certificate faults
findings.why_it_matters: `isinstance(exc, aiohttp.ClientSSLError | ssl.SSLError)` sends any TLS failure to the 5-minute Slow tier. That includes `SSLEOFError` and `SSLZeroReturnError`, which aiohttp wraps as `ClientConnectorSSLError`, a `ClientSSLError`. These are what a client sees when HA's own TLS listener, or a TLS terminator, goes down mid-handshake during a restart. D9 says Slow is for failures that "won't heal without an upstream fix", and only certificate verification failures fit that description. The unit test pins the over-broad rule with a bare `ssl.SSLError("bad record")`. This is a narrower trigger than Finding 4, because a terminator that stays up answers at the HTTP level (502, or 404 as in Finding 4) rather than failing the handshake.
findings.recommended: A: Restrict the Slow TLS match to `ssl.SSLCertVerificationError` and `aiohttp.ClientConnectorCertificateError`. Other SSL errors stay Fast. Update the unit test to pin both sides.
findings.chosen: A: Restrict the Slow TLS match to `ssl.SSLCertVerificationError` and `aiohttp.ClientConnectorCertificateError`. Other SSL errors stay Fast. Update the unit test to pin both sides.

findings.title: A parked never-connected process reports `/api/health` status `starting`, the same as a slow boot
findings.why_it_matters: `get_system_status()` returns `starting` whenever `has_ever_connected` is False, so a parked process looks like a boot in progress. The docs tell operators to alert on `starting` "staying" that way, which means each operator has to invent a time threshold. A Docker healthcheck keyed on `/api/health` sees no failure. D10 weighed a typed health status (option C) and chose A, deferring the typed signal to #1926. The cost lands on every external consumer of `/api/health` until then, and Finding 3's resolution changes how often the state occurs.

findings.title: The RUNNING gate clears lifecycle readiness for a never-connected service, contradicting the invariant `on_initialize` documents
findings.why_it_matters: `on_initialize` and the comment at `:384-385` say lifecycle readiness must not depend on HA, because a startup wave that times out triggers a fatal shutdown. `wait_for_core_running` calls `report_not_ready` unconditionally (`:468`). On a cold start against a booting HA, the common case, this clears `ready_event` through `mark_not_ready` and emits a not-ready event. Anything that later calls `wait_ready` on this service blocks until CONNECTED; one such caller is ServiceWatcher's `await_service_readiness` (`service_watcher.py:644-654`). The critic did not prove that the startup wave's waiter can still be pending when the first `get_config` reply arrives, so this is a timing dependency, not a demonstrated bug.
findings.recommended: A: While the service has never connected, have the gate set the reason and emit a readiness event without clearing `ready_event`.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2

findings.title: A reason change on an already-not-ready service emits no event, so the live Diagnostics view shows a stale reason through the RUNNING wait
findings.why_it_matters: On a reconnect, the drop emits "Not connected to Home Assistant". HA then answers STARTING, and `report_not_ready("...waiting for RUNNING")` writes `_ready_reason` but emits nothing, because `was_ready` is False. The frontend updates `ready_phase` live only from `service_status` events. Its merge prefers WebSocket entries over HTTP data, so even an HTTP refetch doesn't correct the stale "Not connected". An open dashboard during an HA restart is this feature's main scenario. D10 and D12 promise that the reason is visible without reading logs. The Build call (design.md:330) claims visibility "through `ready_phase` without an event", which holds for a polled `/api/health` but not for the live UI.
findings.recommended: A: Emit a readiness event from `report_not_ready` whenever the reason string changes.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2

findings.title: During a first-start outage the never-connected service's reason reads "WebSocket service initialized"
findings.why_it_matters: `handle_connection_failure` replaces the reason only `if was_connected or not self.is_ready()`. A never-connected service is still ready from `on_initialize`, so through a first-start outage (refused, DNS, 502) `ready_phase` reads "WebSocket service initialized". The D11 log says "Cannot reach Home Assistant ... check base_url"; the Diagnostics view says nothing is wrong. This is the opposite pull from Finding 9 on the same state.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2

findings.title: `mark_connected` reads the generation after an await, so it can pass `None` to observers and announce a connection that already died
findings.why_it_matters: `mark_connected` checks `recv_task.done()` only at its top. It then sets CONNECTED and awaits `_emit_readiness_event()`, which awaits a memory-channel send that can yield under load. After that it reads `self._connected_generation` fresh. If the recv task dies with an exception during that await, `_handle_recv_task_done` sets DISCONNECTED, and that transition nulls `_connected_generation` and clears `_connected_event`. `mark_connected` then calls `connected_observers.notify(None)`, although the observer type is `Callable[[int], ...]` and StateProxy's `_needs_connected_synchronization(generation: int)` expects an int. It also emits `WEBSOCKET_CONNECTED` for a dead socket. The loop recovers, so this is a spurious signal plus a type violation, not a hang.
findings.recommended: A: Capture `generation = next(self._generation_seq)` in a local and pass that. Re-check `recv_task.done()` after `_emit_readiness_event()` and before setting `_connected_signal_active`. Add a test that kills the recv task during the readiness emit.
findings.chosen: A: Capture `generation = next(self._generation_seq)` in a local and pass that. Re-check `recv_task.done()` after `_emit_readiness_event()` and before setting `_connected_signal_active`. Add a test that kills the recv task during the readiness emit.

findings.chosen: A: In cleanup, clear `_recv_task` before calling `cancel()`, and make `_handle_recv_task_done` treat a cancelled task that is still `self._recv_task` as a lost connection.

The ledger's six-file docs list (design.md:22) omits both. The first page's failure-behavior table says a WebSocket disconnect gets "ServiceWatcher restart ... within the TRANSIENT budget", and that `InvalidAuthError` triggers "an immediate shutdown". findings.title: The accept-then-drop hot-loop protection has no loop-level test at real pacing
findings.why_it_matters: D8's deciding factor is "never hot-loop when the Supervisor proxy accepts then drops". The unit tests pin the policy math given a `connected_for` value. Every loop-level test, however, runs under `fast_reconnect`, which shrinks the curve to milliseconds, and none drives a server that sends `auth_ok` and then closes. A regression in how `serve()` derives `connected_for` from `_connected_at` would reset the curve on every accept-then-drop and still pass the suite. Shutdown during the Slow sleep or during `park()`, and DNS failure classified as Fast, are also untested.
findings.chosen: In `tests/integration/websocket/test_reconnect_loop.py`, add a test that drives 6+ accept-then-drop cycles: the fake HA sends `auth_ok` (or reaches the gate) and then closes. Record the delays passed to `asyncio.sleep` with the real Fast constants (no `fast_reconnect` cap shrink; patch the sleep or clock instead), and assert that the delays grow to and stay at ≤5 s rather than resetting to ~1 s. Also add a shutdown-while-parked test and a DNS-failure-is-Fast case.
